of inanimate things, e. g. fire, Num. 16,
Zech. 11, 1; comp. ignis edax, Virg.
Æn. 2. 758; πάντας πῦρ ἐσθίει Il. 23.
182. Also of the sword, 2 Sam. 2, 26.
18, 8. Deut. 32, 42; of famine and pesti-
lence Ez. 7, 15; of deadly disease Job
18, 13; of the wrath of God Ex. 15, 7;
of a curse Is. 24, 6; of heat and cold
Gen. 31, 40; of ardent zeal Ps. 69, 10.
3. i. q. to enjoy any thing, e. g. good,
good-fortune, c. בְּ Job 21, 25; the fruits
of good or bad actions, sensual pleasures,
Prov. 30, 20; comp. 9, 17. So Lat. vesci
voluptatibus Cic. Fin. 5. 20.
4. Perh. to taste, to have the sense of
taste, Deut. 4, 28.
5. to eat off, i. e. to take from, to di-
minish. Ez. 42, 5 the upper chambers
were shorter, כִּי יוֹכְלוּ אַתִּיקִים מֵהֵנָה for
the galleries took away from them, i. e.
occupied part of the space.
Niph. נֶאֱכַל, fut. יֵאָכֵל, to be eaten, Ex.
12, 46. 13, 3. 7; also of what may be eat-
en, to be fit for food, Gen. 6, 21. Metaph.
to be devoured by fire, Zech. 9, 4.
Piel אִכֵּל i. q. Kal, like Arab. أَكَّلَ,
to eat up, to consume. Job 20, 26 תְּאָכְלֵהוּ
אֵשׁ a fire consumes him, for תְּאַכְּלֵהוּ.
The Dagesh forte extruded is com-
pensated by the long vowel Kamets;
though some Mss. read תְּאַכְּלֵהוּ. See
Pual to be consumed, with fire Neh.
2, 3. 13; by the sword Is. 1, 20.
Hiph. הֶאֱכִיל, fut. יַאֲכִיל, once 1 pers.
אוֹכִיל Hos. 11, 4; inf. הָכִיל for הַאֲכִיל Ez.
21, 33; pr. to make eat up or consume,
e. g. the sword Ez. 21, 33. Spec. to
give to eat, to feed with any thing, with
two acc. of pers. and thing, Ex. 16, 32.
with מִן of food, Ps. 81, 17.
Deriv. the four following, and אֲכִילָה,
מַאֲכָל, מַאֲכֶלֶת, מַאֲכֹלֶת, מַכֹּלֶת.
אֲכַל Chald. fut. יֵאכֻל, i. q. Heb. to eat,
to devour. אֲכַל קַרְצוֹהִי דִּי pr. to eat the
pieces of any one, to eat him up piece-
meal, metaph. for to slander, to accuse
falsely, to inform against, Dan. 3, 8. 6,
25. So in Targg. אֲכַל קוּרְצִין for Heb.
הָלַךְ רָכִיל, רָגַל. Syr. ܐܶܟܰܠ ܩܰܪ̈ܨܶܐ for Gr.
διαβάλλω Luke 16, 1; whence part. ܐܳܟܶܠ
ܩܰܪܨܳܐ diabolus, Arab. أَكَلَ لحم فلان id.
See also in Chald. קְרַץ.
אֹכֶל m. c. suff. אָכְלוֹ 1. an eating,
devouring, i. e. act of eating, Ex. 12, 4
אִישׁ לְפִי אָכְלוֹ every one according to his
2. food, spec. a) grain, fruits, pro-
duce, provision, Gen. 14, 11. 41, 35 sq.
42, 7 sq. 43, 2 sq. 44, 1. b) prey, meat,
of wild animals, Job 9, 26. 39, 3. 32. [38,
אֻכָל or אֻכָּל pr. n. m. Ucal, Prov. 30, 1;
see in אִיתִיאֵל.
אָכְלָה f. (r. אָכַל) food, Gen. 1, 29. 6,
21; so of the meat or prey of animals
Jer. 12, 9; food i. e. fuel of fire Ez. 15,
אָכֵן adv. pr. inf. absol. Hiph. from r.
כּוּן, for הָכֵן, הָכִין; firmly, Josh. 3, 17.
4, 3. Chald. הָכִין, הָכֵי. Others, i. q.
כֵּן with א prosthetic.
1. Strongly affirming, surely! truly!
of a certain truth! Gen. 28, 16. Ex. 2,
2. Adversat. but, yet, Ps. 31, 23. Is. 49,
* אָכַף 1. to load up a beast of bur-
den, pr. prob. to bend, to make bow down
under a load, kindr. with כָּפַף q. v. Arab.
أَكَّفَ II, to bind fast the pack-saddle;
IV, to put on the pack-saddle. See de-
riv. אֶכֶף.—Hence
2. to impel to labour, to urge on, like
Syr. ܐܶܟܰܦ. Once Prov. 16, 26 כִּי אָכַף
עָלָיו פִּיהוּ for his mouth urges him on,
i. e. his hunger drives him to labour.
The construction with עַל is to be ex-
plained from the primary signif. of lay-
ing on a load.
אֶכֶף m. a load, burden; hence me-
taph. weight, dignity, authority, like
כָּבוֹד. Job 33, 7 וְאַכְפִּי עָלֶיךָ לֹא יִכְבָּד and
my dignity shall not weigh heavy upon
thee. So Chald. Syr. But Sept. ἡ χείρ
μου, and so Kimchi, regarding אֶכֶף i. q.
כַּף in the similar passage Job 13, 21.
The former sense is to be preferred.
* אָכַר a root not in use, i. q. Arab.
أَكَرَ Conj. V, to dig, espec. the earth;

line_status.note: The kaf is printed with a dagesh (dot visible inside the letter), as the context requires — the Mss. retain the Dagesh forte rather than compensating with Kamets — so תְּאַכְּלֵהוּ, not the defective-dagesh form in B.
Two separate dots are actually printed after "16" before "Is." (a typographical doubled period), so Reading A matches the print; B silently normalises it to one.

Four items are printed (A drops מַאֲכֶלֶת, the segol-form), but B lists them in reversed order: in print, left to right, the sequence is מַאֲכָל, מַאֲכֶלֶת, מַאֲכֹלֶת, מַכֹּלֶת, with the full stop at the far right after מַכֹּלֶת (dagesh in kaf confirmed).

Visually the line runs left→right: רָגַל , הָלַךְ רָכִיל . — so the Hebrew run in logical (RTL) order begins with הָלַךְ רָכִיל, then the comma, then רָגַל, as in Reading A; Reading B inverted the item order. The Syriac second word carries a two-dot seyame over rish (plural, matching Targ. קוּרְצִין), which B omitted. Vowel points as in A.

The first word is Syriac Serto ܩܪܨܐ (qarṣā, completing ܐܟܠ ܩܪܨܐ "diabolus" from the previous line), with a pthaha printed over qoph and a zqapha over the end; Reading A misread the Serto letters as Arabic مُنْزِا. In the Arabic phrase, فلان carries no fatha on the lam.

The final letter is final pe (ף), not final kaf with sheva (ךְ): there is no sheva beneath it, and the shape has the inward-curling pe stroke. The middle letter is a rounded kaf (no bet heel), matching the root אכף confirmed by the kindred כָּפַף and Arabic أكف on the following lines. Reading A is correct.
The kāf carries a shadda (the ع-shaped mark) with fatḥa above it, as expected for a form II verb — Reading A omits the shadda.

The Syriac word carries two Western vowel signs, one above the alaph (rbasa) and a second distinct sign above the kaph (pthaha), with no plain dot anywhere; Reading B's zqapha on alaph plus a bare dot over kaph does not match the two shaped vowel marks printed. The Hebrew אָכַף (qamets, patah) is identical in both and matches the print.

The vowel under the dageshed bet of the last Hebrew word is a qamets (horizontal with a descending tick), not a pathach; this matches the Masoretic reading יִכְבָּד in Job 33:7. All other points agree in both readings.

Second letter is a kaf: its base is flush with the top stroke with no rightward heel protruding past the body as a bet would have; this agrees with the following Arabic cognate أكر (kaf) and the entry’s sense “to dig” (אִכָּר husbandman).

The printed Arabic has only three letters — alif (with hamza and fatha), kaf, ra — with simple fathas above; there is no initial tāʾ and no shadda on the kāf, so Reading B's تَأَكَّرَ is not what is printed.
